varied_dimension: place preposition before a full street address with a house number (at vs on vs in vs onto)
prompt: Choose the word or phrase that correctly completes the sentence.
passage: Stargazing club newsletter: from next month, our meetings will be held in the small observatory ________ 214 Orion Avenue.
explanation: We use "at" with a complete address that includes a house number (at 214 Orion Avenue). "On" is used with a street name alone (on Orion Avenue), and "in" is used with larger areas such as cities.

distractor_rationales.in: "In" goes with cities, areas and the inside of a building, not with an address that has a number.
distractor_rationales.on: "On" goes with a street name alone (on Orion Avenue); once the house number is added, the address takes "at".
distractor_rationales.onto: "Onto" shows movement to a surface; nothing moves here, so it cannot introduce a location.

student_error.in: The sentence already says "in the small observatory", so learners repeat "in" for the address too.
student_error.on: Learners correctly learn "on + street" and keep it even when a house number turns the street into an exact address.
student_error.onto: Learners who translate one general place word from their first language treat "onto" as a stronger form of "on".

varied_dimension: which preposition comes before relative 'which', decided by the verb at the end of the clause (depends on)
prompt: Choose the word or phrase that correctly completes the sentence.
passage: "The star chart ________ our whole club depends was drawn by Ms. Ishikawa many years ago," our planetarium guide explained.
explanation: The verb "depend" always takes "on" (the club depends on the chart). When the chart becomes a relative clause, the preposition moves to the front with it: "the chart on which our club depends".

distractor_rationales.which: Without a preposition, "depends" is left with nothing to connect it to the chart; the verb needs "on".
distractor_rationales.with which: "Depend" never takes "with"; "with which" fits verbs such as "work" or "help".
distractor_rationales.about which: "About which" fits verbs such as "talk" or "write", not "depend".

student_error.which: Learners use plain "which" for every object relative clause and forget the preposition the verb needs.
student_error.with which: Learners whose first language uses a 'with' word after 'rely' or 'depend' carry that preposition into English.
student_error.about which: Learners treat "about" as an all-purpose preposition for any topic or thing being discussed.

varied_dimension: forms of the root 'harm' (harm / harms / harmful / harmless), decided by the contrast after 'but'
prompt: Choose the word or phrase that correctly completes the sentence.
passage: The guide said, "Looking at the Moon is ________, but the Sun can hurt your eyes."
explanation: After "is" we need an adjective. "But" shows a contrast with the Sun, which can hurt your eyes, so the Moon must be safe: "harmless" means "not causing harm", while "harmful" means "causing harm".

distractor_rationales.harmful: "Harmful" is the right word class but the wrong meaning; it would say the Moon hurts your eyes too, so "but" would make no sense.
distractor_rationales.harms: "Harms" is a verb; after "is" the sentence needs an adjective.
distractor_rationales.harm: "Harm" is a noun or a verb, not an adjective, so it cannot describe "looking at the Moon" after "is".

student_error.harmful: Learners mix up -ful and -less and remember only that both words are about harm.
student_error.harms: Learners see a subject and add a verb ending without noticing that "is" is already the verb.
student_error.harm: Learners use the root word for every form because their first language does not change the word's shape.

varied_dimension: double comparative: 'much more' placed before an adjective that already ends in -er
prompt: Choose the underlined word or phrase that is NOT correct.
passage: Through Jabari's telescope, [A: Jupiter looked much more] bigger [B: than it] [C: did] [D: in the pictures].
explanation: "Bigger" is already a comparative, so it cannot also take "more". "Much" can strengthen a comparative on its own: "Jupiter looked much bigger".

distractor_rationales.than it: "Than" correctly follows a comparative, and "it" correctly refers back to Jupiter.
distractor_rationales.did: "Did" correctly replaces "looked" and matches the past tense of the sentence.
distractor_rationales.in the pictures: "In" is the correct preposition for things shown in pictures.

student_error.than it: Learners wonder whether the pronoun should be "its" or whether "then" is meant.
student_error.did: Learners expect the verb "looked" to be repeated and doubt the short auxiliary.
student_error.in the pictures: Learners often choose "on the pictures" because pictures are flat surfaces.

varied_dimension: 'would rather' takes a bare infinitive, contrasted with 'would love' + to-infinitive
prompt: Choose the underlined word or phrase that is NOT correct.
passage: [A: I would love] [B: to see Mars], but tonight I would rather [C: to go] [D: to the planetarium].
explanation: "Would rather" is followed by the base form of the verb without "to": "I would rather go". "Would love", like "would like", does take "to": "I would love to see Mars".

distractor_rationales.I would love: "Would love" is a correct, polite way to say what you want.
distractor_rationales.to see Mars: "Would love" is correctly followed by a to-infinitive.

student_error.I would love: Learners think "would" must be followed only by a bare verb and doubt "would love" as a phrase.
student_error.to see Mars: After learning that modals take a bare verb, learners wrongly remove "to" after "would love" as well.
student_error.to the planetarium: Learners are unsure whether "go" takes "to" or "at" before a building.

varied_dimension: 'too + adjective' must be followed by a to-infinitive, not an -ing form
prompt: Choose the underlined word or phrase that is NOT correct.
passage: Liesel said the comet [A: was] [B: too faint] [C: spotting at all] [D: without a strong telescope].
explanation: The pattern is "too + adjective + to + verb": the comet was too faint to spot at all. An -ing form cannot follow "too faint" here.

distractor_rationales.was: "Was" correctly matches the past verb "said" and the singular subject "comet".

student_error.was: Learners think reported speech must keep the speaker's present tense ("is").
student_error.too faint: Learners confuse "too" and "very" or put "enough"-style word order here.
student_error.without a strong telescope: Learners wonder whether "without" needs "using" or another verb after it.

varied_dimension: modal passive missing 'be' (must + past participle instead of must be + past participle)
prompt: Choose the underlined word or phrase that is NOT correct.
passage: Stargazing club newsletter: [A: Our telescopes] [B: that we lent] [C: to the new members last week] must [D: brought back by Friday].
choices: to the new members last week
explanation: The telescopes do not bring anything back; someone brings them back, so the verb must be passive. A passive after a modal is "modal + be + past participle": "must be brought back by Friday".

distractor_rationales.Our telescopes: The plural subject correctly matches the plural relative clause and modal phrase.
distractor_rationales.that we lent: "Lent" is the correct irregular past of "lend", and "that" correctly introduces the clause.
distractor_rationales.to the new members last week: "Lend something to someone" is correct, and "last week" fits the past verb "lent".

student_error.Our telescopes: Learners wonder whether a possessive pronoun can come before a noun that has a long relative clause after it.
student_error.that we lent: Learners confuse "lend" and "borrow" and are unsure of the irregular past "lent".
student_error.to the new members last week: Learners doubt whether "lend" takes "to" or "for" before the person.

varied_dimension: -ing adjective used for a person's feeling where the -ed form is needed (fascinating by vs fascinated by)
prompt: Choose the underlined word or phrase that is NOT correct.
passage: After [A: watching the show], [B: most of] the visitors [C: from Oksana's school] [D: were extremely fascinating] by the rings of Saturn.
explanation: An -ed adjective describes how a person feels, and an -ing adjective describes the thing that causes the feeling. The visitors felt the interest caused by the rings, so they were "extremely fascinated by" them.

distractor_rationales.watching the show: After the preposition "after", the -ing form "watching" is correct.
distractor_rationales.most of: "Most of the" + plural noun is correct.
distractor_rationales.from Oksana's school: "From" correctly shows where the visitors came from, and the possessive is correct.

student_error.watching the show: Learners think a full clause or a to-infinitive is needed after "after".
student_error.most of: Learners often drop "of" and write "most the visitors", so they doubt the correct form.
student_error.from Oksana's school: Learners are unsure whether to write "of" or "from" and where the apostrophe goes.

varied_dimension: 'unless' (condition) used where the time limit 'until' is needed with a durative main clause
prompt: Choose the underlined word or phrase that is NOT correct.
passage: [A: Unless the clouds cleared], we [B: waited outside] the observatory for nearly an hour, [C: while Benedikt] [D: told us old stories about the constellations].
choices: told us old stories about the constellations
explanation: "Unless" means "if not" and introduces a condition. The sentence describes waiting that ended when the clouds cleared, which is a time limit, so it needs "until": "Until the clouds cleared, we waited outside".

distractor_rationales.waited outside: The past simple fits a finished event, and "outside" correctly comes before "the observatory".
distractor_rationales.while Benedikt: "While" correctly shows that the storytelling happened during the waiting.
distractor_rationales.told us old stories about the constellat: "Tell" + person + thing is correct, and "stories about" is the right preposition.

student_error.waited outside: Learners expect "waited for" or "outside of" and doubt the plain form.
student_error.while Benedikt: Learners confuse "while" with "whereas" and think "while" can only show contrast or needs an -ing verb.
student_error.told us old stories about the constellat: Learners mix up "tell" and "say" and wonder whether "to us" is needed.

varied_dimension: reflexive pronoun must agree with a compound subject joined by 'and' (themselves, not himself)
prompt: Choose the underlined word or phrase that is NOT correct.
passage: Do-yun and his sister [A: have taught] [B: himself] [C: the names of all eight planets] [D: by using] a phone app.
choices: the names of all eight planets
explanation: A reflexive pronoun refers back to the whole subject. "Do-yun and his sister" is two people, so the pronoun must be plural: "have taught themselves".

distractor_rationales.have taught: The plural "have" agrees with the compound subject, and "taught" is the correct irregular participle.
distractor_rationales.the names of all eight planets: "All eight planets" is correct word order, and "names of" is correct.
distractor_rationales.by using: After the preposition "by", the -ing form is correct.

student_error.have taught: Learners match the verb to the nearest noun "sister" and expect "has", or doubt the irregular form "taught".
student_error.the names of all eight planets: Learners are unsure whether to write "all the eight planets" or "eight all planets".
student_error.by using: Learners think a preposition must be followed by a to-infinitive or a bare verb ("by use").

varied_dimension: two objects of 'explains' must both be that-clauses; the first is a noun + -ing phrase
prompt: Choose the underlined word or phrase that is NOT correct.
passage: Akosua's report explains [A: Venus being] hotter than Mercury, [B: although] it is farther from the Sun, and [C: that its clouds] [D: trap most of] the heat.
explanation: The two things the report explains are joined by "and", so they must have the same form. The second is a that-clause ("that its clouds trap ..."), so the first must be one too: "explains that Venus is hotter than Mercury".

distractor_rationales.although: "Although" correctly introduces a surprising contrast: Venus is hotter even though it is farther away.
distractor_rationales.that its clouds: "That" begins a correct noun clause, and "its" is the correct possessive (not "it's").
distractor_rationales.trap most of: The plural verb "trap" agrees with "clouds", and "most of the" is correct.

student_error.although: Learners confuse "although" with "because" or "despite" and doubt the contrast.
student_error.trap most of: Learners match the verb to "Venus" or "its" and expect "traps".

varied_dimension: 'will' not backshifted to 'would' when the reported future ('the next evening') is already past
prompt: Choose the underlined word or phrase that is NOT correct.
passage: Two weeks ago, the planetarium guide [A: said] that the meteor shower [B: will peak] [C: the next evening] and [D: could be seen] without a telescope.
explanation: The guide spoke two weeks ago about the next evening, a time that is now in the past, so "will" must move back to "would": "would peak the next evening". The second verb, "could be seen", is already correctly backshifted from "can".

distractor_rationales.said: "Said that" correctly introduces reported speech without a person as object.
distractor_rationales.the next evening: In reported speech, "tomorrow evening" correctly becomes "the next evening".
distractor_rationales.could be seen: "Can be seen" correctly backshifts to "could be seen" in past reported speech.

student_error.said: Learners mix up "said" and "told" and think a person ("said us") or "to us" is required.
student_error.the next evening: Learners keep the speaker's words "tomorrow evening" and doubt the changed time phrase.
student_error.could be seen: Learners think the passive with a modal needs "been" or that "can" should stay unchanged.

varied_dimension: singular subject followed by 'as well as' + plural phrase still takes a singular verb
prompt: Choose the underlined word or phrase that is NOT correct.
passage: Samira, [A: as well as] her three teammates, [B: are hoping to sketch] the eclipse [C: from the roof] [D: of their school] on Saturday.
explanation: A phrase starting with "as well as" or "along with" adds information but does not change the subject. The subject is only "Samira", so the verb must be singular: "Samira, as well as her three teammates, is hoping to sketch". Only "and" would make the subject plural.

distractor_rationales.as well as: "As well as" correctly adds the teammates as extra information.
distractor_rationales.from the roof: "Sketch from" correctly shows the place where the artists are.
distractor_rationales.of their school: "Their" correctly refers to all four people, who go to the same school.

student_error.as well as: Learners think "as well as" is only used at the end of a sentence, like "as well".
student_error.from the roof: Learners expect "on the roof" and doubt "from".
student_error.of their school: Learners think the pronoun should be "her" because the subject is singular.
